public_rationale: In April 2025, OpenAI's own system card reported hallucination rates of 33% (o3) and 48% (o4-mini) on its PersonQA test. Both were worse than the older o1, and OpenAI said more research was needed to understand why. The same month, the independent lab Transluce found that o3 often made up actions it had taken and defended the fabrications when challenged. In May 2025, the LA Times reported about 30 lawyer cases that year involving AI-generated errors in court filings. Together these show that hallucination was a material, unsolved problem for leading generative AI at the time of the post. 'Deep' and 'serious' are judgments, but the evidence fits the plain reading.
limitations: Hallucination rates depend heavily on the benchmark. Some models and tasks show much lower rates.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Hallucination is a deep, serious, unsolved problem with generative AI.

statement.excerpt: Take hallucinations, a deep, serious, unsolved problem with Generative AI, which I have been warning about since 2001.
statement.document_title: AI literacy, hallucinations, and the law: A case study

our_interpretation: Read as a claim about the state of generative AI at the post date (May 2025): leading models still hallucinated at material rates, and no developer had shown a fix.

'Deep, serious' is a judgment. Plain reading: material hallucination rates on published evaluations from leading labs, plus documented real-world harm. 'Unsolved' means no lab claimed or showed that hallucinations had been eliminated.
The part about warning since 2001 is biographical and is not scored.
criteria.support_condition: Evaluations of frontier models from around April–May 2025 show substantial hallucination rates, and documented incidents of harmful fabrication continued at that time.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evaluations from that period show frontier models with negligible hallucination rates, or credible evidence that the problem had been solved by May 2025.
